Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo; 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': absolute path (no ~) to the built .app bundle (e.g. /Users/me/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/MyApp-abc123/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

# PUMS RELSHIPP codes for the householder (20) and the householder's relatives by birth,
# marriage or adoption: spouses (21, 23), children (25-27), siblings (28), parents (29),
# grandchildren (30), in-laws (31, 32) and other relatives (33). Unmarried partners (22, 24),

HOUSEHOLDER = 20
RELATIVES = {21, 23, *range(25, 34)}

                 categories: dict[str, str] = CATEGORIES) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Blank values are outside a column's universe:
    - household_id: group-quarters residents, who live in no household
    - family_id: everyone outside a Census family (see family_ids)
    - EDUCATION: under 25; EMPLOYMENT: under 16
    - POVERTY, POVERTY_RATIO: people whose poverty status is not determined (institutions,
      college dorms, military quarters, unrelated children under 15)
    """
    missing = [c for c in fields.values() if c not in seed.columns]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"the cached PUMS persons lack {missing}; refetch with `synthpop fetch --only pums_persons`")
    joined = _join_seed(persons, seed, list(fields.values()))
    out = pd.DataFrame({
        "person_id": joined["person_id"],
        "family_id": family_ids(persons, seed).reset_index(drop=True),
        "parcel_id": joined["parcel_id"],
    })
    for name, col in fields.items():
        out[name] = joined[col].map(LABELS[name]) if name in LABELS else joined[col].astype("Int64")
    for name, col in categories.items():
        if col in persons.columns:
            out[name] = persons[col].astype("string").to_numpy()
    out["household_id"] = joined["household_id"].where(joined["household_id"] >= 0).astype("Int64")

You're using about a tenth of the PUMS file. I didn't have the Census data dictionary locally, so I read the column headers of the raw files (`psam_p23.csv`, `psam_h23.csv`) and measured each variable on Portland's 4,185 people and 2,453 households (PUMA 01000).

**What you use now** ([sources/__init__.py:36](synthpop/sources/__init__.py:36)):
- **People:** age, sex, race, Hispanic origin, education, relationship to the householder, poverty ratio and employment status.
- **Households:** size, group quarters or not, building type, tenure, year built, bedrooms, home value and household income.
- **Downloaded but unused:** household income, home value, year built and bedrooms never reach the person table.

## How a new variable can come in

1. **Copied from the seed person (cheap).** Every synthetic person is a full copy of one PUMS record, so a new column is one entry in `PERSON_COLS` and `FIELDS` in [persons.py:22](synthpop/persons.py:22). It stays consistent with that person's age, poverty and so on. The catch: it is only right across the whole PUMA, not block by block.
2. **Copied and fitted to an ACS table.** Add it as a constraint in `config/variables.yaml` as well, and it will vary correctly by neighbourhood. That depends on the ACS publishing the table at block-group level; some are tract-only.

## What's there, with Portland figures

| Group | Variables | Portland (weighted) | Fit by neighbourhood? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Disability** | any disability, plus hearing, vision, cognitive, walking, self-care and independent living | 13% any; 6% walking; 6% cognitive | Tract only, I believe |
| **Health insurance** | insured, public coverage, Medicaid | 5% uninsured; 33% public; 17% Medicaid | Tract only, I believe |
| **Income** | person income, wages, Social Security, SSI, public assistance; household income (already downloaded) | median person income $36.5k | Household income: yes, block group |
| **Housing costs** | rent, rent as % of income, owner costs | median rent $1,300; median rent burden 30% | Rent burden: yes |
| **Work and commute** | class of worker, occupation (372 codes), industry, hours, travel mode, minutes to work | 66% drive, 22% work from home, 8% walk; median 15 min | Commute mode: yes |
| **Cars and internet** | vehicles, internet access, high-speed internet | 13% of households have no car; 5% no internet | Yes, both |
| **Language and origin** | born abroad, citizenship, language at home, English ability, limited-English household, ancestry, birthplace | 11% born abroad; 11% speak another language; 3% limited-English households | Mostly yes |
| **Household make-up** | family type, children, people 65+, multigenerational, partner, workers in family | 28% of households have someone 65+; 17% have children | Yes, several |
| **Other** | marital status, veteran, in school or grade, moved in the last year, food stamps (SNAP), birth in the last year, grandparent caregiver | 6% veterans; 15% moved last year; 10% of households on SNAP | Mixed |

The `F…` columns also say whether the Census imputed each answer, which could become a quality flag in the person table.

## Things to watch

- **Small sample.** Rare groups rest on only a few PUMS records. For example, the English-ability question applies to just 9% of people, and multigenerational households are 1%. They'll show up as the same few people copied many times.
- **Codes need grouping.** Occupation, industry and ancestry have hundreds of codes; they'd need folding into about 8 groups before they can colour the map.
- **Household variables need a new path.** They join on `SERIALNO` rather than the person, which is easy but new.

My suggestion:
- **Start with copied variables, no fitting:** disability, insurance, person income, veteran and language. They give you data points like "65+ with a walking difficulty and no car" right away.
- **Then fit the three that matter most by neighbourhood:** commute mode, vehicles and internet access, all of which the ACS publishes by block group.

"""Data points: health or other measures attached to synthetic people by a risk model,
computed live and optionally saved.

    model = RiskModel.parse({...})
    engine = DataPointEngine(out_dir, catalog, city_id)
    frame = engine.compute(model, "block_group")   # area_id, estimate, se, share, share_se, confidence
    store = DataPointStore("config/datapoints.yaml", catalog)   # or "s3://bucket/key"

A risk model gives every synthetic person a probability:

    logit p = logit(baseline) + Σ log(odds ratio of the person's category, per factor)

`baseline` is the prevalence for the reference person (every factor at a category
with no odds ratio). People outside the universe get p = 0 and are not counted
in shares. An area's estimate is its expected number of cases, so values add up
across levels exactly as the other variables do. Uncertainty combines placement
spread (21 draws) and survey spread (80 replicates), as in summarize.py. It does
not include uncertainty in the odds ratios themselves.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import json
import math
import re
import threading
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import yaml

from .catalog import Catalog
from .publish import risk_factors
from .store import Document
from .summarize import confidence

ID_PATTERN = re.compile(r"^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{1,40}$")


@dataclass
class RiskModel:
    id: str
    label: str
    baseline: float                                  # prevalence for the reference person, 0–1
    odds_ratios: dict[str, dict[str, float]] = field(default_factory=dict)
    universe: dict[str, list[str]] = field(default_factory=dict)   # factor -> categories counted
    description: str = ""
    source: str = ""

    @classmethod
    def parse(cls, raw: dict, catalog: Catalog) -> "RiskModel":
        factors = {f: set(catalog.variable(f).category_ids) for f in risk_factors(catalog)}
        m = cls(id=str(raw["id"]), label=str(raw.get("label") or raw["id"]), baseline=float(raw["baseline"]),
                odds_ratios={f: {c: float(v) for c, v in cats.items()} for f, cats in (raw.get("odds_ratios") or {}).items()},
                universe={f: [str(c) for c in cats] for f, cats in (raw.get("universe") or {}).items()},
                description=str(raw.get("description", "")), source=str(raw.get("source", "")))
        if not ID_PATTERN.match(m.id):
            raise ValueError("id must be lower_snake_case, 2–41 characters, starting with a letter")
        if not 0 < m.baseline < 1:
            raise ValueError("baseline must be a prevalence between 0 and 1 (exclusive)")
        for f, cats in {**m.odds_ratios, **{k: dict.fromkeys(v, 1) for k, v in m.universe.items()}}.items():
            if f not in factors:
                raise ValueError(f"unknown factor {f!r}; use one of {sorted(factors)}")
            bad = set(cats) - factors[f]
            if bad:
                raise ValueError(f"unknown {f} categories {sorted(bad)}")
        for f, cats in m.odds_ratios.items():
            for c, v in cats.items():
                if not 0 < v < 1000:
                    raise ValueError(f"odds ratio for {f}={c} must be between 0 and 1000")
        return m

from conftest import BG_IN, BG_OUT, TRACT


def test_geography_is_clipped_to_the_study_area(sources):

    assert parcels.crs.to_epsg() == 4326

    assert {"WGTP1", "WGTP80"} <= set(hh.columns) and {"PWGTP1", "PWGTP80"} <= set(pp.columns)
    assert len(pp) == 7


def test_acs_keeps_study_levels_and_cleans_jam_values(sources):
    acs = sources.load("acs")
    by_level = acs.groupby("level")["area_id"].unique().to_dict()

    assert list(by_level["county"]) == ["23005"] and list(by_level["state"]) == ["23"]
    assert list(by_level["city"]) == ["2399999"]
    first = acs[acs["cell"] == "B01001_001"]
    assert (first["moe"] == 0).all()             # -555555555 means controlled, so zero error

def build_fixtures(root: Path) -> Path:
    root.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    left = box(X0, Y0, X0 + W / 2, Y0 + W)
    right = box(X0 + W / 2, Y0, X0 + W, Y0 + W)
    outside = box(X0 + W, Y0, X0 + 2 * W, Y0 + W)

    _shapefile_zip(gpd.GeoDataFrame({"PLACEFP": ["99999", "11111"], "GEOID": ["2399999", "2311111"],
                                     "NAME": ["Fixtureville", "Elsewhere"]},
                                    geometry=[box(X0, Y0, X0 + W, Y0 + W), outside], crs=4326),
                   root / "tiger_place.zip")
    _shapefile_zip(gpd.GeoDataFrame({"COUNTYFP": ["005", "005"], "GEOID": [TRACT, "23005000200"],
                                     "NAMELSAD": ["Census Tract 1", "Census Tract 2"]},
                                    geometry=[box(X0, Y0, X0 + W, Y0 + W), outside], crs=4326),
                   root / "tiger_tract.zip")
    _shapefile_zip(gpd.GeoDataFrame({"COUNTYFP": ["005"] * 3, "GEOID": BG_IN + [BG_OUT],
                                     "NAMELSAD": ["Block Group 1", "Block Group 2", "Block Group 1"]},
                                    geometry=[left, right, outside], crs=4326),
                   root / "tiger_bg.zip")

    blocks = []
    for bg, cell in ((BG_IN[0], left), (BG_IN[1], right), (BG_OUT, outside)):
        x0, y0, x1, y1 = cell.bounds
        mid = (y0 + y1) / 2
        for i, b in enumerate((box(x0, y0, x1, mid), box(x0, mid, x1, y1))):
            blocks.append({"GEOID20": f"{bg[:11]}{bg[11]}{i:03d}", "COUNTYFP20": "005", "POP20": 20 + i,
                           "HOUSING20": 10 + i, "ALAND20": 1000, "geometry": b})
    _shapefile_zip(gpd.GeoDataFrame(blocks, crs=4326), root / "tiger_blocks.zip")

    parcels, points = [], []
    for j, blk in enumerate(blocks):

                               "PLACE_TYPE": "Apartment" if k else "Single Family", "MAP_BK_LOT": pid,
                               "ZIPCODE": "04101", "TOWN": "Fixtureville", "geometry": Point(c.x, c.y)})
    parcels.append({"Parcel_ID": "P00", "geometry": box(X0, Y0, X0 + 0.0001, Y0 + 0.0001)})  # split lot

# Maine synthetic population

**Live demo:** https://ma-5ce4446f22454607ad16ee51e42c72f0.ecs.us-east-2.on.aws (its front page explains how to use the map and read the numbers)

A parcel-level synthetic population for Portland, Maine, built only from public Census and State of Maine data, with an interactive 3D map. Every value is a **synthetic estimate**, not a record of real people.

- Architecture: [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md)
- Module design: [docs/design.md](docs/design.md)
- Validation report: [docs/validation.md](docs/validation.md)
- Scaling plan: [docs/scaling.md](docs/scaling.md)
- Risks and open questions: [docs/risks.md](docs/risks.md)
- Terms: [GLOSSARY.md](GLOSSARY.md)

## Setup

You need [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), Python 3.12+ and Node 20+. No API keys are needed.

```bash
uv sync
uv run synthpop fetch        # download, clip and cache every input into data/ (about 2 minutes)
uv run synthpop build        # model runs, area stats, docs/validation.md, published files (about 3 minutes)
(cd app && npm install && npm run build)
uv run synthpop serve        # API and map at http://localhost:8000
uv run pytest                # tests run on a built-in fixture town, offline
(cd app && npm test)         # front-end tests: the people, households and map view (vitest)
```

The build steps can also run one at a time: `synthpop run`, `summarize`, `validate`, `publish`. Delete files in `data/interim/` to refetch an input.

**Front-end development:** run `uv run synthpop serve`, then `cd app && npm run dev` and open http://localhost:5173. Vite forwards `/api` and `/geo` to port 8000.

## Deploy

The app is one process: FastAPI serves the API, the geometry files and the built front end, and reads only `data/out/` (about 78 MB for Portland, a third of it the people of all 102 runs for the simulation player). After building the data:

```bash
docker build --platform linux/arm64 -t maine-synthpop .
docker run -p 8000:8000 -e SYNTHPOP_PASSWORD=try-me maine-synthpop
```

Three environment variables configure a deployment:

- `SYNTHPOP_PASSWORD` turns on basic auth (user `SYNTHPOP_USER`, default `synthpop`). `/healthz` stays open for load-balancer health checks.
- `SYNTHPOP_DATAPOINTS` sets where saved data points live. Use `s3://bucket/key` in a container, or saves are lost on redeploy.

[docs/deploy-aws.md](docs/deploy-aws.md) has step-by-step commands for AWS ECS Express Mode (Fargate on Graviton, HTTPS load balancer, S3, Secrets Manager), at about $80 a month (about $2.70 a day for a short demo). Any other container host works too. Keep one server copy while saved data points are in a single file.

## What's where

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `config/variables.yaml` | The variable schema: variables, categories, ACS constraints |
| `config/study_area.yaml` | Study area, data vintages, model settings |
| `synthpop/sources/` | Fetch, clip and cache public data |
| `synthpop/model/` | Fitting, placement and runs |
| `synthpop/summarize.py` | Area stats with standard errors |
| `synthpop/validate.py` | The validation report |
| `synthpop/publish.py`, `atlas.py`, `api.py` | Published files, queries, HTTP routes |
| `app/` | deck.gl + MapLibre front end |
| `docs/` | Architecture, design, validation report, ADRs |

## Data points: health measures, live

In the app's **Data points** section, start a new data point, or start from a preset such as Alzheimer's dementia from Dhana et al. 2023. A data point is a risk model:
- a baseline prevalence for a reference person;
- odds ratios by age, sex, race/ethnicity, education and living quarters;
- the ages it counts.

Every synthetic person gets a probability, and each area shows its expected cases and rate with margins. Moving any slider redraws the map and the rate-by-group charts within a fraction of a second.

**Save as variable** writes the model to `config/datapoints.yaml`. It then works like any other variable (colour, filters, detail panel, export) with no rebuild. **×** removes it. The live maths uses per-run person counts that `synthpop publish` writes (`cells_draws.parquet`, `cells_reps.parquet`). The margins cover the synthetic population's uncertainty, not uncertainty in the odds ratios.

## Adding a variable

Add an entry to [config/variables.yaml](config/variables.yaml):
- a **seed** variable recoded from a PUMS column, or
- a **derived** variable built from other variables' categories.

Then rebuild. The variable appears in the API and the map without code changes.

Every input is public, needs no login and no API key. Each is clipped to the study area, reprojected to EPSG:4326 and cached in `data/interim/` as (Geo)Parquet.

| Source | What we take | Portland result |
|---|---|---|
| [ACS PUMS 2020–2024 5-year](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/data/pums/2024/5-Year/), Maine | Household and person records for PUMA 23-01000 (Portland, South Portland, Westbrook), with all 80 replicate weights | 2,453 housing records (1,859 occupied households), 4,185 persons (442 in group quarters) |
| [ACS 2020–2024 5-year table-based summary files](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/) | Tables B01001, B03002, B11016, B15003, B25002, B25008, B25032, streamed and filtered without storing the national files | 61 block groups, 20 tracts, plus city, county and state rows (11,760 values) |
| [TIGER/Line 2024](https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/TIGER2024/) place, tracts, block groups | Boundaries. Areas count as Portland if at least half their area is inside the city. | 1 city, 20 tracts, 61 block groups |
| [TIGER/Line 2020 tabulation blocks](https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/TIGER2020/TABBLOCK20/) | Block boundaries with 2020 Census population and housing-unit counts | 1,065 blocks, 68,336 people, 35,591 housing units |
| [Maine GeoLibrary statewide parcels](https://services1.arcgis.com/RbMX0mRVOFNTdLzd/ArcGIS/rest/services/Parcels/FeatureServer/38) | Parcel boundaries and IDs (no assessor attributes) | 31,321 parcels |
| [Maine E911 address points](https://services1.arcgis.com/RbMX0mRVOFNTdLzd/ArcGIS/rest/services/Maine_E911_Addresses_Feature/FeatureServer/0) | Address, unit, place type, parcel key | 40,708 points. 76.6% match a parcel ID by key; the rest are joined by location. |

Checks on the fetched data: the 61 block groups sum to 68,761 people against 68,854 for the city (99.9%). The 2020 blocks sum to 68,336 against the city's 2020 count of 68,408.

The variables, constraint tables and category mappings all live in `config/variables.yaml`. Every ACS cell ID in it was checked against the official table shells (`ACS20245YR_Table_Shells.txt`).

## 2. Model (`synthpop build`, next)

For the main run, 20 more placement draws of it, 80 replicate runs (one per PUMS replicate weight set) and one validation run, in every block group:

1. **Fit.** A penalized maximum-entropy fit (P-MEDM style, [ADR 0002](adr/0002-penalized-entropy-fit.md)) reweights the PUMA's seed households and group-quarters persons to that block group's ACS totals: sex × age, race/ethnicity, education (25+), household vs group quarters, household size, and tenure × units in structure.

"""Fitting seed units to block-group totals, and turning weights into whole units.

`fit_weights` is penalized maximum-entropy calibration, the idea behind P-MEDM
(Nagle et al.; used by UrbanPop): find weights as close as possible to the seed
weights (in relative entropy) such that every ACS total is met to within roughly
its own standard error. Noisy, slightly inconsistent ACS cells therefore pull
less than precise ones instead of forcing an impossible exact fit.

It is solved in the dual with Newton's method:

    w(λ) = w0 · exp(Aᵀλ / γ)
    minimize  γ Σ w(λ) − tᵀλ + ½ Σ s² λ²,   γ = n / N²

At the optimum the miss on each cell is A·w − t = −s²·λ. A[c, u] is how much
unit u contributes to cell c (1 for a household cell, the number of matching
people for a person cell), so household and person totals are fitted together.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass

import numpy as np

MIN_SE = 1.0          # every cell may miss by about one unit; keeps the problem well conditioned
MIN_WEIGHT = 1e-3     # replicate weights can be zero or negative; keep every seed unit usable


@dataclass
class Fit:
    weights: np.ndarray
    fitted: np.ndarray        # A @ weights, per cell
    iterations: int
    converged: bool
    max_rel_error: float      # largest |fitted − target| / max(target, 1)


def fit_weights(A: np.ndarray, w0: np.ndarray, targets: np.ndarray, se: np.ndarray | None = None, min_se: float = MIN_SE,
                max_iter: int = 200, tol: float = 1e-8) -> Fit:
    t = np.maximum(np.asarray(targets, dtype=float), 0)
    s2 = np.maximum(np.zeros_like(t) if se is None else np.asarray(se, dtype=float), min_se) ** 2
    w0 = np.maximum(np.asarray(w0, dtype=float), MIN_WEIGHT)
    hh_like = A.max(axis=0) > 0
    # Start from seed weights scaled to the right overall size, so λ only reshapes.
    scale = t.max() / max((A @ w0).max(), 1e-9)
    w0 = w0 * scale
    # P-MEDM weighs relative entropy over proportions by n/N (n seed units, N people).
    # Over counts that is n/N², which lets ACS totals, not the seed, set the size.
    gamma = len(w0) / max(t.max(), 1.0) ** 2

    lam = np.zeros(len(t))

    def dual(l):
        w = w0 * np.exp(np.clip(A.T @ l / gamma, -40, 40))
        return gamma * w.sum() - t @ l + 0.5 * (s2 * l * l).sum(), w

    f, w = dual(lam)
    converged = False
    it = 0
    for it in range(1, max_iter + 1):
        g = A @ w - t + s2 * lam
        H = (A * w) @ A.T / gamma + np.diag(s2)
        step = np.linalg.solve(H, g)
        alpha = 1.0
        while alpha > 1e-8:
            f_new, w_new = dual(lam - alpha * step)
            if f_new <= f - 1e-4 * alpha * (g @ step):
                break
            alpha /= 2
        lam, f, w = lam - alpha * step, f_new, w_new
        if np.abs(alpha * step).max() < tol * (1 + np.abs(lam).max()):
            converged = True
            break
    w = np.where(hh_like, w, 0.0)
    fitted = A @ w
    err = float(np.max(np.abs(fitted - t) / np.maximum(t, 1.0))) if len(t) else 0.0
    return Fit(w, fitted, it, converged, err)


def integerize(weights: np.ndarray, rng: np.random.Generator) -> np.ndarray:
    """Truncate, then sample the fractional remainder without replacement, so the
    integer total equals the rounded weight total."""
    w = np.maximum(weights, 0)
    counts = np.floor(w).astype(int)
    rem = w - counts
    k = int(round(rem.sum()))
    if k > 0:
        pick = rng.choice(len(w), size=min(k, int((rem > 0).sum())), replace=False, p=rem / rem.sum())
        counts[pick] += 1
    return counts

# 2. Penalized maximum-entropy fitting (P-MEDM style), not plain IPF

The plan was plain IPF first, with P-MEDM (the UrbanPop method) as a later upgrade. The first test showed that plain IPF and IPU can't fit person totals that cut across households. They scale every unit in a cell by the same factor, so they can't shift weight between households that differ only in size. On real Portland data the fit also missed totals by 20–25%.

So `model.fit.fit_weights` solves a penalized maximum-entropy problem, the same formulation as P-MEDM. It keeps weights as close as possible to the PUMS weights, in relative entropy weighted by n/N as P-MEDM does, while letting each ACS cell miss by about its standard error. It is solved in the dual with Newton's method: one small linear system per iteration (62 cells), about 10 iterations per block group.

On Portland's main run:
- 99.8% of block-group cells fall within 1 SE.
- 100% fall within the ACS 90% margin of error.
- City totals are within 0.7% for households and 2.2% for people.

A run takes under a second.

What is still missing compared with UrbanPop's P-MEDM: tract-level constraints alongside block-group ones, and allocation probabilities as an output. Both fit behind the same `model.run(inputs, run)` interface.

content.text:
## Diabetes data

I pulled diabetes data for all 20 Portland tracts from **CDC PLACES** (2025 release, based on the 2023 BRFSS survey). It's the measure "diagnosed diabetes among adults". The ACS microdata has no diabetes question, so PLACES is the standard public source at tract level.

- **Tracts:** from 5.6% (tract 12) to 11.5% (tract 24), each with a 95% interval.
- **City:** 8.3% crude, 8.1% age-adjusted. The tracts, weighted by their 58,078 adults, average 8.29%, so the tract and city figures agree.
- **County:** 8.9% crude, 7.4% age-adjusted. Portland's population is younger than the county's.

**Where it lives:**
- It's a new source in [sources/__init__.py](synthpop/sources/__init__.py), cached at `data/interim/places.parquet`.
- `uv run synthpop fetch --only places` refetches it.
- To pull more measures (obesity, COPD, depression and so on), add their ids to `PLACES_MEASURES`.
- The release year is set in `config/study_area.yaml`.
- There's a fixture test, and the source table is in [architecture.md](docs/architecture.md).

Nothing reads this data yet, so it's not on the map.

## A better way to do the penalized entropy fit?

The method itself is sound; it's the same family as UrbanPop's P-MEDM. The weak spot is how you use it: each of the 61 block groups is fitted **on its own**. That's also the first gap your own decision record ([0002-penalized-entropy-fit.md](docs/adr/0002-penalized-entropy-fit.md)) lists. In order of payoff:

1. **Fit all block groups of a tract together, against tract and block-group tables at once.** This is the original P-MEDM setup (Nagle et al.). The same dual Newton solver works, just with a larger matrix of constraints. It gives you:
   - tract-only tables as constraints, such as disability and health insurance, which you can't use now;
   - block groups that add up to their tract;
   - less noise in small block groups, because tract totals are much more precise.
2. **Start each block group from a better prior.** Today every block group starts from the same PUMA-wide seed weights. Starting from the tract's fitted weights instead (a hierarchical prior) keeps neighbourhoods realistic where block-group tables are noisy.
3. **Add neighbouring PUMAs to the seed, at a lower weight.** With 4,185 people, rare combinations (older, limited English, no car) come from only a handful of records copied many times. A larger pool gives the fit more distinct people to choose from.
4. **Tune the penalty.** The penalty strength and `MIN_SE = 1` are fixed today. They can be chosen by leaving one ACS table out of the fit and checking how well it's predicted.

**Alternatives I'd skip:**
- **IPF/IPU and GREG-style calibration:** IPF and IPU already failed here (they missed totals by 20–25%), and calibration estimators like GREG are a variation on what you already have.
- **Generating new records with a Bayesian network or VAE:** this does create combinations missing from the seed, but you lose real, internally consistent PUMS records. That matters for the person table.

**How this connects to diabetes:** PLACES can't be a constraint in the fit, because PUMS people have no diabetes value. Instead, it becomes a diabetes data point with odds ratios by age, sex, race, education and poverty, whose baseline is adjusted in each tract so the tract's expected cases match its PLACES rate. Today's data points use one baseline for the whole city, so this needs a per-tract baseline. The joint tract fit from option 1 also makes those tract counts more accurate.

"""Synthesis and placement.

    inputs = model.prepare(data, catalog, area)     # once
    placed = model.run(inputs, Run.main())          # or Run.draw(d), Run.replicate(r), Run.validation(...)

Every run fits seed units to each block group's ACS totals (IPU), turns the
weights into whole households and group-quarters residents, and places every
household on exactly one parcel. Totals at every level therefore add up.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from ..catalog import Catalog
from ..config import StudyArea
from .fit import Fit, fit_weights, integerize
from .place import capacity, gq_block_weights, parcel_base, place_group_quarters, place_households

__all__ = ["Run", "Inputs", "Placed", "prepare", "run", "holdout_blocks"]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Run:
    kind: str                         # "main", "draw", "replicate" or "validation"
    r: int = 0                        # replicate weight set, 1..80 for replicate runs
    holdout: frozenset[str] = frozenset()
    d: int = 0                        # placement draw; replicate and validation runs share draw 0 with main

    @classmethod
    def main(cls) -> "Run":
        return cls("main")

    @classmethod
    def draw(cls, d: int) -> "Run":
        """The main run with a different placement draw (same weights and targets)."""
        if d < 1:
            raise ValueError("placement draws are numbered from 1")
        return cls("draw", 0, frozenset(), d)

    @classmethod
    def replicate(cls, r: int) -> "Run":
        if not 1 <= r <= 80:
            raise ValueError("replicate runs are numbered 1 to 80")
        return cls("replicate", r)

    @classmethod
    def validation(cls, holdout: frozenset[str]) -> "Run":
        return cls("validation", 0, frozenset(holdout))

    @property
    def name(self) -> str:
        return {"replicate": f"replicate_{self.r:02d}", "draw": f"draw_{self.d:02d}"}.get(self.kind, self.kind)


@dataclass
class Inputs:
    catalog: Catalog
    area: StudyArea
    units: pd.DataFrame               # one row per seed unit: unit kind, serial, structure
    members: pd.DataFrame             # seed persons with categories and their unit index
    A: np.ndarray                     # cells x units incidence
    cells: pd.DataFrame               # constraint, key, unit, acs cells
    weights: np.ndarray               # 81 x units: column 0 main weights, then replicates 1..80
    targets: pd.DataFrame             # block groups x cells, estimates
    target_se: pd.DataFrame           # block groups x cells, standard errors
    parcels: pd.DataFrame             # parcel_base(): block, block group, raw units, gq site
    blocks: pd.DataFrame              # 2020 blocks without geometry
    avg_household_pop: pd.Series      # people per housing unit, by block group (ACS)


@dataclass
class Placed:
    run: Run
    households: pd.DataFrame          # household_id, seed_serial, parcel_id, block, block_group, match, category columns
    persons: pd.DataFrame             # person_id, household_id, parcel_id, block, block_group, category columns
    capacity: pd.DataFrame            # units per parcel used by this run
    fits: pd.DataFrame                # per block group: iterations, converged, max error
    fitted: pd.DataFrame = field(default=None)   # block groups x cells, synthetic totals after integerizing


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------- prepare

def prepare(data: dict, catalog: Catalog, area: StudyArea) -> Inputs:
    persons, households = catalog.apply(data["pums_persons"], data["pums_households"])

    hh_units = households[(households["TYPEHUGQ"] == 1) & (households["NP"] > 0)].copy()
    hh_units["kind"] = "household"
    gq_people = persons[persons["living_quarters"] == "group_quarters"].copy()
    gq_units = pd.DataFrame({"SERIALNO": gq_people["SERIALNO"].to_numpy(), "kind": "group_quarters",
                             "SPORDER": gq_people["SPORDER"].to_numpy()})
    units = pd.concat([hh_units.assign(SPORDER=0), gq_units], ignore_index=True)
    units["unit"] = np.arange(len(units))

    hh_index = dict(zip(hh_units["SERIALNO"], units.loc[units["kind"] == "household", "unit"]))
    members = persons.copy()
    members["unit"] = members["SERIALNO"].map(hh_index)
    gq_mask = members["living_quarters"] == "group_quarters"
    members.loc[gq_mask, "unit"] = units.loc[units["kind"] == "group_quarters", "unit"].to_numpy()
    members = members[members["unit"].notna()].copy()
    members["unit"] = members["unit"].astype(int)

    cells = []
    for c in catalog.constraints:
        for key, acs in c.cells.items():
            cells.append({"constraint": c.id, "key": key, "unit_kind": c.unit, "by": c.by, "acs": acs,
                          "exact": c.exact})
    cells = pd.DataFrame(cells)

    A = np.zeros((len(cells), len(units)))
    unit_cats = units.merge(households, on="SERIALNO", how="left", suffixes=("", "_h"))
    for i, cell in cells.iterrows():
        values = cell["key"].split("|")
        if cell["unit_kind"] == "household":
            mask = np.ones(len(units), dtype=bool) & (units["kind"] == "household").to_numpy()
            for col, val in zip(cell["by"], values):
                mask &= (unit_cats[col].astype(str) == val).to_numpy()
            A[i] = mask
        else:
            m = np.ones(len(members), dtype=bool)
            for col, val in zip(cell["by"], values):
                m &= (members[col].astype(str) == val).to_numpy()
            A[i] = np.bincount(members.loc[m, "unit"], minlength=len(units))

    weights = np.zeros((81, len(units)))
    is_hh = (units["kind"] == "household").to_numpy()
    gq_w = gq_people.reset_index(drop=True)
    for r in range(81):
        hcol, pcol = ("WGTP", "PWGTP") if r == 0 else (f"WGTP{r}", f"PWGTP{r}")
        weights[r, is_hh] = hh_units[hcol].to_numpy()
        weights[r, ~is_hh] = gq_w[pcol].to_numpy()

    acs = data["acs"][data["acs"]["level"] == "block_group"]
    est = acs.pivot(index="area_id", columns="cell", values="estimate")

    """Sum (and subtract) ACS cells for every constraint cell. MOEs combine as the
    root sum of squares, the Census approximation for sums and differences."""
    t, s = {}, {}
    for i, cell in cells.iterrows():
        total = 0
        var = 0
        for ref in cell["acs"]:
            sign = -1 if ref.startswith("-") else 1
            ref = ref.lstrip("-")
            total = total + sign * est[ref].fillna(0)
            var = var + (moe[ref].fillna(0) / 1.645) ** 2

        s[i] = np.sqrt(var)

        n[~is_hh] = integerize(fit.weights[~is_hh], rng)

        fitted[bg] = inputs.A @ n
        fits.append({"block_group": bg, "iterations": fit.iterations, "converged": fit.converged,
                     "max_rel_error": fit.max_rel_error})

    units = inputs.units
    rows = []
    for bg, n in counts.items():
        idx = np.repeat(np.flatnonzero(n), n[n > 0])
        rows.append(pd.DataFrame({"unit": idx, "block_group": bg}))
    drawn = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
    drawn["copy_id"] = np.arange(len(drawn))
    drawn = drawn.merge(units[["unit", "kind", "SERIALNO", "structure"]], on="unit")

    cap = capacity(inputs.parcels, inputs.blocks, spec.holdout)
    parcel_info = cap.set_index("parcel_id")[["block"]]

    hh = drawn[drawn["kind"] == "household"].rename(columns={"copy_id": "household_id", "SERIALNO": "seed_serial"})
    placed = place_households(hh[["household_id", "block_group", "structure"]], cap, rng)
    hh = hh.merge(placed, on="household_id")
    hh["block"] = parcel_info.loc[hh["parcel_id"], "block"].to_numpy()

    gq = drawn[drawn["kind"] == "group_quarters"].copy()
    weights = gq_block_weights(inputs.blocks, inputs.avg_household_pop, spec.holdout)
    gq["parcel_id"] = place_group_quarters(gq, cap, weights, rng).to_numpy() if len(gq) else []

    # seed_serial + seed_person name the PUMS person each synthetic person copies,
    # so any PUMS column (exact age, poverty, ...) can be joined back later.
    m = inputs.members[["unit", "SERIALNO", "SPORDER"] + person_cols].rename(
        columns={"SERIALNO": "seed_serial", "SPORDER": "seed_person"})
    hp = hh[["household_id", "unit", "parcel_id", "block", "block_group"]].merge(m, on="unit")
    gp = gq[["copy_id", "unit", "parcel_id", "block", "block_group"]].merge(m, on="unit").drop(columns="copy_id")
    gp["household_id"] = -1
    persons = pd.concat([hp, gp], ignore_index=True).drop(columns="unit")
    persons.insert(0, "person_id", np.arange(len(persons)))

    hh_cats = inputs.units[["unit"] + hh_cols]
    households = hh.drop(columns=["structure"]).merge(hh_cats, on="unit").drop(columns=["unit", "kind"])

    fitted_df = pd.DataFrame(fitted).T
    fitted_df.columns = inputs.targets.columns
    return Placed(spec, households, persons, cap, pd.DataFrame(fits), fitted_df)

household on exactly one parcel. Totals at every level therefore add up.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Run:
    kind: str                         # "main", "draw", "replicate" or "validation"
    r: int = 0                        # replicate weight set, 1..80 for replicate runs
    holdout: frozenset[str] = frozenset()
    d: int = 0                        # placement draw; replicate and validation runs share draw 0 with main

    @classmethod
    def main(cls) -> "Run":
        return cls("main")

    @classmethod
    def draw(cls, d: int) -> "Run":
        """The main run with a different placement draw (same weights and targets)."""
        if d < 1:
            raise ValueError("placement draws are numbered from 1")
        return cls("draw", 0, frozenset(), d)

    @classmethod
    def replicate(cls, r: int) -> "Run":
        if not 1 <= r <= 80:
            raise ValueError("replicate runs are numbered 1 to 80")
        return cls("replicate", r)

    @classmethod
    def validation(cls, holdout: frozenset[str]) -> "Run":
        return cls("validation", 0, frozenset(holdout))

    @property
    def name(self) -> str:
        return {"replicate": f"replicate_{self.r:02d}", "draw": f"draw_{self.d:02d}"}.get(self.kind, self.kind)

    members["unit"] = members["SERIALNO"].map(hh_index)
    gq_mask = members["living_quarters"] == "group_quarters"
    members.loc[gq_mask, "unit"] = units.loc[units["kind"] == "group_quarters", "unit"].to_numpy()
    members = members[members["unit"].notna()].copy()
    members["unit"] = members["unit"].astype(int)

    cells = []
    for c in catalog.constraints:

    cells = pd.DataFrame(cells)

    A = np.zeros((len(cells), len(units)))

    for i, cell in cells.iterrows():

            mask = np.ones(len(units), dtype=bool) & (units["kind"] == "household").to_numpy()
            for col, val in zip(cell["by"], values):
                mask &= (unit_cats[col].astype(str) == val).to_numpy()

            m = np.ones(len(members), dtype=bool)
            for col, val in zip(cell["by"], values):
                m &= (members[col].astype(str) == val).to_numpy()
            A[i] = np.bincount(members.loc[m, "unit"], minlength=len(units))

    weights = np.zeros((81, len(units)))
    is_hh = (units["kind"] == "household").to_numpy()

    base = parcel_base(data["parcels"], data["e911"], data["blocks"])
    occupied = est["B25002_002"].replace(0, np.nan)
    avg_household_pop = (est["B25008_001"] / occupied).fillna(2.0)
    return Inputs(catalog, area, units, members, A, cells, weights, targets, se, base, blocks, avg_household_pop)

# Validation report

Synthetic estimates for Portland, Maine, aggregated from parcels, compared with published Census figures. Generated by `synthpop validate`; do not edit by hand.

## Headline

- **City people**: 68,673 ± 370 synthetic vs 68,854 ± 52 ACS (90% margins; difference -0.3%)
- **City households**: 33,338 ± 491 synthetic vs 32,965 ± 785 ACS (90% margins; difference +1.1%)
- **City people 65+**: 11,501 ± 857 synthetic vs 11,616 ± 772 ACS (90% margins; difference -1.0%)
- **Block-group cells inside the ACS 90% margin**: 99.9% of 5,469
- **Held-out blocks, population share**: correlation 0.84 with 2020 Census (land-area baseline 0.68) across 162 blocks

## 1. Fit to published ACS, by level

Synthetic counts from the main run, summed up from parcels, against ACS 2020–2024 published estimates. RAE (relative allocation error, as in UrbanPop) is |synthetic − published| / published 90% MOE, so RAE ≤ 1 means the synthetic value is inside the published margin. Block groups are what the model fits to. Tracts and the city are independent ACS estimates, so they test whether block-group fits add up correctly. Tracts that extend beyond the study area are left out. Two expected gaps: housing units are 2020 Census block counts while ACS covers 2020–2024, and the study area is the 61 block groups at least half inside the city, which hold 93 fewer people than the city's own ACS total.

id: str
    label: str
    kind: str
    unit: str
    categories: tuple[Category, ...]
    rules: tuple[tuple[str, str], ...] = ()      # (category, pandas query)
    bins: dict | None = None                     # {"column": ..., "edges": [[lo, hi], ...]}
    universe: str | None = None
    source: dict | None = None                   # attached variables only

    @property
    def category_ids(self) -> list[str]:
        return [c.id for c in self.categories]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Constraint:
    id: str
    unit: str
    by: tuple[str, ...]
    cells: dict[str, tuple[str, ...]]            # "male|a0_4" -> ("B01001_003", "-B25008_001")
    exact: bool = False                          # fit as a hard total instead of within its SE

    @property
    def tables(self) -> set[str]:
        return {c.lstrip("-").split("_")[0] for cells in self.cells.values() for c in cells}


@dataclass
class Catalog:
    levels: list[str]
    variables: list[Variable]
    constraints: list[Constraint]
    model_tables: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- loading

    @classmethod
    def load(cls, path: str | Path) -> "Catalog":
        raw = yaml.safe_load(Path(path).read_text())
        variables = [_parse_variable(v) for v in raw["variables"]]
        ids = [v.id for v in variables]
        if len(ids) != len(set(ids)):
            raise ValueError(f"duplicate variable ids in {path}")
        known = set(ids)
        constraints = []
        for c in raw.get("constraints", []):
            missing = [b for b in c["by"] if b not in known]
            if missing:
                raise ValueError(f"constraint {c['id']} uses unknown variables {missing}")
            constraints.append(Constraint(
                id=c["id"], unit=c["unit"], by=tuple(c["by"]),
                cells={k: tuple(v) for k, v in c["cells"].items()}, exact=bool(c.get("exact", False)),
            ))
        return cls(levels=raw["levels"], variables=variables, constraints=constraints,
                   model_tables=list(raw.get("model_tables", [])))

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- lookups

    def variable(self, id: str) -> Variable:
        for v in self.variables:
            if v.id == id:
                return v
        raise KeyError(id)

    @property
    def active(self) -> list[Variable]:
        """Variables the build computes (attached ones wait for an attach step)."""
        return [v for v in self.variables if v.kind != "attached"]

    @property
    def acs_tables(self) -> list[str]:
        tables = set(self.model_tables)
        for c in self.constraints:
            tables |= c.tables
        return sorted(tables)

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pytest

from synthpop import model
from synthpop.model import Run
from synthpop.model.fit import fit_weights, integerize
from shapely.geometry import Point

from synthpop.model.place import assign_points
from synthpop.persons import family_ids, locate, person_table
from conftest import AREA


@pytest.fixture
def inputs(sources, catalog):
    return model.prepare(sources.load_all(), catalog, AREA)


def test_fit_hits_consistent_household_and_person_targets():
    # 3 household types; cells: households of type a, b; persons total.
    A = np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 1], [1, 2, 3]], dtype=float)
    fit = fit_weights(A, np.ones(3), np.array([10, 20, 70]), se=np.full(3, 1e-3), min_se=1e-3)
    assert fit.converged
    np.testing.assert_allclose(A @ fit.weights, [10, 20, 70], rtol=1e-3)


def test_integerize_keeps_the_rounded_total():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    w = np.array([0.4, 1.7, 2.2, 0.7])
    assert integerize(w, rng).sum() == round(w.sum())


def test_every_household_lands_on_one_parcel_in_its_block_group(inputs):
    placed = model.run(inputs, Run.main())
    hh, cap = placed.households, placed.capacity.set_index("parcel_id")
    assert hh["household_id"].is_unique
    assert hh["parcel_id"].notna().all()
    assert (cap.loc[hh["parcel_id"], "block_group"].to_numpy() == hh["block_group"].to_numpy()).all()
    per_parcel = hh[hh["match"] != "overflow"].groupby("parcel_id").size()
    assert (per_parcel <= cap.loc[per_parcel.index, "units"]).all()


def test_people_match_their_households(inputs):
    placed = model.run(inputs, Run.main())
    in_hh = placed.persons[placed.persons["household_id"] >= 0]
    sizes = in_hh.groupby("household_id").size()
    expected = placed.households.set_index("household_id")["household_size"].map(
        {"p1": 1, "p2": 2, "p3": 3, "p4": 4}).dropna()
    assert (sizes.reindex(expected.index) == expected).all()
    # every person sits on the same parcel as their household
    merged = in_hh.merge(placed.households[["household_id", "parcel_id"]], on="household_id", suffixes=("", "_hh"))
    assert (merged["parcel_id"] == merged["parcel_id_hh"]).all()


def test_person_table_copies_exact_age_and_sex_from_the_seed(inputs, sources):
    placed = model.run(inputs, Run.main())
    table = person_table(placed.persons, sources.load("pums_persons"))
    assert list(table.columns) == ["person_id", "family_id", "parcel_id", "AGE", "SEX", "RACE", "EDUCATION",
                                   "POVERTY", "POVERTY_RATIO", "EMPLOYMENT", "household_id"]

'''## Update: tract and block groups fitted together

`model.fit.fit_tract` now fits all block groups of a tract at once. Each block group is still fitted to its own cells. The tract's own ACS totals are added as extra cells on the block groups' sum, which is P-MEDM's multilevel form. The objective is the sum of the block groups' separate objectives plus the tract cells' misses, so with no tract cells it gives exactly the old per-block-group fit (a test checks this).

The Hessian has a block structure, one A·diag(w/γ)·Aᵀ per block group, so a tract of four block groups costs about four separate fits. A main run went from 0.6 s to 0.8 s.

Only tracts whose block groups are all in the study area get tract cells: 19 of Portland's 20. Tract 23005002400 has one of its three block groups outside the city, so its block groups are fitted on their own. `model.fit_tracts: false` in `config/study_area.yaml` turns the joint fit off.

On Portland, against the published ACS (the validation report):
- Median tract RAE fell for every variable. For example, age 0.05 → 0.03, race/ethnicity 0.05 → 0.03, structure 0.10 → 0.07 and tenure 0.11 → 0.09.
- Block-group fit stayed at 99.9% inside the margin.
- The city 65+ margin fell from ±857 to ±547.
- Block-level coefficients of variation fell slightly: 80% of blocks are high confidence, up from 77%.

The gain is modest because ACS block-group estimates already add up closely to their tracts. The bigger payoff is that the fit can now take tables published only for tracts, such as disability and health insurance.

**Caveat on margins.** A tract estimate and its block groups' estimates come from the same survey responses. Treating them as independent cells, as P-MEDM does, counts some of that information twice. The narrower replicate margins are therefore somewhat optimistic. Replicate runs also perturb tract and block-group targets independently.

Still missing compared with UrbanPop's P-MEDM: allocation probabilities as an output.''')

content.text:
I added a joint tract-and-block-group fit. Each tract's block groups are now fitted together, with the tract's own ACS totals added on their sum. Everything got a little better, and the full build was redone with the new fit. The gain is modest, though, because the ACS block-group numbers already add up closely to their tracts.

**How it works**
- `fit_tract` in [fit.py](synthpop/model/fit.py) fits a whole tract's block groups at once. `fit_weights` is now its one-block-group case.
- With no tract totals it gives exactly the old per-block-group result: on real Portland data the weights matched the old code to within 1e-12, and a test checks this.
- It stays fast: a tract of four block groups costs about four separate fits, and a run went from 0.6 s to 0.8 s.
- 19 of the 20 tracts are fitted jointly. Tract 23005002400 has one of its three block groups outside the city, so its block groups are still fitted on their own.
- `fit_tracts: false` in `config/study_area.yaml` switches back to the old fit.

**Before and after** (validation report, rebuilt):

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Tract error, median (age / race / structure / tenure) | 0.05 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.11 | 0.03 / 0.03 / 0.07 / 0.09 |
| Block-group cells inside the ACS margin | 99.9% | 99.9% |
| City 65+ margin | ±857 | ±547 |
| Blocks graded high confidence | 77% | 80% |
| Held-out blocks, population correlation | 0.84 | 0.82 |

Things to know:
- **The narrower margins are somewhat optimistic.** A tract estimate and its block groups come from the same survey answers. Counting both, as P-MEDM does, counts some information twice. I wrote this up in [ADR 0002](docs/adr/0002-penalized-entropy-fit.md).
- **The held-out block correlation dipped from 0.84 to 0.82.** That figure measures placement, which I didn't change. Different household counts give different random placements, so I believe it's noise, but I haven't checked that.
- **The real payoff is still to come.** The fit can now use tables the ACS publishes only for tracts, such as disability and health insurance. That would make those columns accurate by neighbourhood, not just across the PUMA.

The diabetes source from earlier is part of the same uncommitted changes. Nothing is committed, and the live site still runs the old version.
